option-a.rationale: Barker clearly denies that secular morality is mere opinion and makes the Job case a concrete test of divine goodness. However, ‘objective reality’ and the claim that morality can be measured are left materially undefined, so the standard connecting observable harm to moral fact remains compressed even though the challenge itself is easy to reconstruct.

option-b.rationale: The claim “Moral value can be objectively justified by real-world harm, and that standard condemns the treatment of Job despite promised compensation.” is recoverable and auditable, though its stated inference is more compressed than the wording suggests.

moveEvidence.speaker: Dan Barker
moveEvidence.claim: Moral value can be objectively justified by real-world harm, and that standard condemns the treatment of Job despite promised compensation.
moveEvidence.warrant: Barker denies morality is mere opinion, says it can be measured against objective reality, and applies the criterion to Job's torture and the death of his children; Horn replies that infinite compensation can follow temporal bad.
moveEvidence.inference: A secular moral standard can make factual moral judgments and continues to challenge the goodness of attributed divine acts.

sourceSpan.excerpt: and I hope people don't change their minds. No, we don't say it's an opinion. We say it is a value that is justified by objective reality. It's not an opinion. You can actually measure morality objectively, not because you feel like something. So when God... Where is it? An objective moral value is an oxymoron. I think you know that. I said moral fact. Well, moral fact, okay. So when God tortured Job for no reason, he said for no reason at all, he admitted it, was that a good thing to do? Was it good to torture a man and kill his ten children? He ordered Satan to do it. Was that a good thing for God to do? It was bad for Job, but because God is all-powerful, he can infinitely compensate any bad things we endure, and so God can give us perfect eternal goodness.

option-a.rationale: The move supplies relevant particulars: the recurring appearance framing, vanishing episodes, and Paul's later visionary encounter jointly support a non-bodily alternative. Its evidential force remains limited because the linguistic and chronological assertions are largely stated rather than documented or comparatively defended, and the move does not show that this reading accounts for the reported group appearances.

option-b.rationale: The stated warrant is source-specific; however, vocabulary and Paul are relevant, but semantic and dating claims lack support.

sourceSpan.excerpt: When Paul says that Jesus appeared to Peter and to the 500, that word appeared is a curious word. If I went to your house and you opened the door and I said, oh, I went to Trent's house and Trent appeared unto me, you would think I was talking about a haunted house, right, or a ghost or something. In all of the gospels before that point, people met people, they saw people, they were with people, they traveled. But after the resurrection, it switches to that Greek participle, ophi, which is where we get the word vision from, basically. It was an appearance. And yet he appeared to these people and he appeared, it was kind of like a spooky vanishing act kind of thing. It's not what you would expect of a resurrected body where you'd go up and shake his hand. And of course, Paul's own experience with Jesus was at least 25 years after the fact in the clouds. What was Jesus hanging up there? Did he grow a beard? What did he do for that whole time? Did Paul actually meet Jesus physically? No. He had a visionary experience. This hardly counts as good history.
